notes: from_ingredient: the ingredient the recipe calls for (the one being substituted).
to_ingredient: the ingredient used in its place.
Directionality is explicit — A→B and B→A are separate entries and may differ in ratio and impact.
Baking-invalid swaps (e.g. oil for butter) are scoped to context='savory' to prevent incorrect baking suggestions.
confidence: 0.000–1.000; reflects how closely the substitute reproduces the original's culinary role.
All ingredient names must match a row in the ingredients catalog.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1 cup whole milk + 1 tbsp lemon juice or white vinegar; stir and let stand 5 min until slightly curdled
substitutions.impact_note: Closely mimics buttermilk's acidity and tenderizing effect in pancakes, cakes, and quick breads.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1; Greek yogurt is the closest match
substitutions.impact_note: Nearly identical fat content and acidity. Greek yogurt is a near drop-in; regular yogurt is slightly thinner.
Sour cream is richer and thicker; expect a creamier, slightly less tangy result.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1 by volume; stir in 1 tbsp flour or cornstarch per cup to compensate for reduced body
substitutions.impact_note: Significantly lower fat content; sauce will be thinner and less rich. Not suitable for whipping.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¾ cup olive oil per 1 cup butter
substitutions.impact_note: Lacks milk solids for browning; adds a distinct olive flavor. Unsuitable for baking where butter's emulsifying role matters.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¾ cup canola oil per 1 cup butter
substitutions.impact_note: Neutral flavor avoids olive character; still lacks milk solids for browning and pastry structure.
Tangier and noticeably thinner. Good in dips and sauces; not reliable in cheesecake or other baked applications.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1 with full-fat Greek yogurt
substitutions.impact_note: Much thinner and more tart; works in dips and dressings but will water down baked applications.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1; blend or whisk first for a smooth texture
substitutions.impact_note: Richer and thicker than sour cream; loses the bright tang but adds body to sauces and dips.
Neutral flavor; loses olive character entirely. Suitable for high-heat cooking where olive flavor would burn off anyway.
Adds a mild olive flavor that can overpower delicate baked goods; appropriate in savory applications only.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¾ cup honey per 1 cup sugar; reduce other liquids by 3 tbsp and add ¼ tsp baking soda per cup of honey used
substitutions.impact_note: Honey adds floral notes and keeps baked goods moister; baking soda neutralizes honey's natural acidity.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1 cup sugar + ¼ cup liquid per ¾ cup honey removed
substitutions.impact_note: Loses floral complexity and moisture-retaining properties; the result will be slightly drier.
Adds subtle molasses flavor and slightly more moisture; works especially well in cookies and muffins.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1; optionally stir 1 tsp molasses into each cup of white sugar to approximate depth
substitutions.impact_note: Loses molasses richness; the result will be slightly less moist and less complex.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¼ tsp baking soda per 1 tsp baking powder; the recipe must contain an acidic ingredient (buttermilk, yogurt, citrus, or cocoa)
substitutions.impact_note: Works only if the recipe has enough acid to activate the soda; a soapy taste results if the baking soda is not fully neutralized.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use 3 tsp baking powder per 1 tsp baking soda
substitutions.impact_note: Provides leavening without requiring acid in the recipe; the larger volume can slightly dilute other flavors.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1 by juice volume
substitutions.impact_note: Limes have a slightly more tropical, floral note and are marginally less tart; nearly interchangeable in most recipes.

substitutions.ratio_note: 1:1 by juice volume
substitutions.impact_note: Lemons are slightly more tart with a cleaner citrus character; the flavor shift is subtle in cooked dishes.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use equal volume of fresh lemon juice
substitutions.impact_note: Brighter, more citrus-forward acidity; loses the mild apple-fruit note and slight funkiness of ACV.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use equal volume of ACV
substitutions.impact_note: Loses citrus aromatics; adds mellow, slightly fruity acidity. Works in marinades, dressings, and acidulated water.
Loses sharp nutty cheddar flavor; gains a better melt and stretch. Add a pinch of dry mustard powder to approximate sharpness.
Sharper flavor and firmer texture; loses the characteristic stretch and mild milky taste of mozzarella.
Sweeter and less earthy; works well in Italian-style sauces and Mediterranean dishes.
Earthier and more robust; reduce by ¼ in delicate sauces to avoid overpowering.
More floral and woody; excellent in soups, stews, and braises.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ½ tsp rosemary per 1 tsp thyme; crush or chop finely first
substitutions.impact_note: Much more assertive piney flavor; best reserved for robust dishes like roasted meats and root vegetables.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use 2 tsp thyme per 1 tsp rosemary; thyme is considerably milder
substitutions.impact_note: Softer, more versatile flavor; loses the distinctive piney intensity of rosemary.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use 3–4 tsp chili powder per 1 tsp cayenne
substitutions.impact_note: Significantly less heat per teaspoon; adds complexity from cumin, garlic, and other spices in the blend.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¼ tsp cayenne per 1 tsp chili powder; cayenne is substantially hotter
substitutions.impact_note: Loses earthy, cumin-forward complexity; adds pure capsaicin heat without the broader spice blend character.
Adds notable heat and spice complexity beyond paprika's mild sweetness; use only when some heat increase is acceptable.
Loses all heat; paprika contributes mild sweetness and color but not the depth of a chili spice blend.
Loses garlic pungency and gains onion sweetness; acceptable only when neither onion nor garlic is critical to the dish.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ½ tsp cinnamon per 1 tsp ginger
substitutions.impact_note: Cinnamon is sweeter and lacks ginger's peppery heat; works in autumnal spice cakes and cookies but not in ginger-forward desserts.
Loses earthy bitterness and vivid golden color; ginger adds warmth and a slight zing. Best limited to curries and Asian-inspired dishes.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use 2 tsp cinnamon per 1 tsp nutmeg
substitutions.impact_note: Sweeter and less pungent; works well in apple-based and autumnal desserts.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¼–½ tsp nutmeg per 1 tsp cinnamon; nutmeg is significantly more potent
substitutions.impact_note: Nutmeg is more complex and pungent; use sparingly. Excellent in custards, cream pies, and spice cakes.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use ¼ tsp salt per 1 tbsp soy sauce removed
substitutions.impact_note: Provides only saltiness; loses all umami depth, fermented complexity, and color that soy sauce contributes.

substitutions.ratio_note: Use 1 tbsp soy sauce per ¼ tsp salt
substitutions.impact_note: Adds umami depth and darkens the dish; can shift the flavor profile significantly toward Asian or savory-forward.

substitutions.ratio_note: Crack 1 tsp whole peppercorns to yield approximately 1 tsp ground; use a mortar, spice grinder, or pepper mill
substitutions.impact_note: Freshly cracked peppercorns are noticeably more aromatic and vibrant than pre-ground; this is an improvement in quality.
